name: Asparagus Green
lede: Asparagus green is a pale, greyed yellow-green from Werner's 1774 colour nomenclature for mineralogists, named for the vegetable but much quieter than a fresh spear.

sections.title: A vegetable's name
sections.body: Paterson defines asparagus as the green of the vegetable and notes that the color is also written asparagus-green [1]. In English a 1790s list that Baty reproduces carries both *asparagus-green* and *sparrow-grass-green* [2]. Baty reports that the second term was new in Kirwan's mineralogy of 1794, and calls it debatable whether it matched grass green [3].

sections.title: Werner's number 58
sections.body:
Abraham Gottlob Werner, a German mineralogist, published a standard list of colour names in 1774 so that students could describe specimens the same way [3][4]. In 1814 the Scottish artist Patrick Syme expanded it to 108 terms [5]. His edition of 1821 reached 110, and he added animal and vegetable examples to Werner's minerals, and a painted swatch for each [5].

In Syme's 1821 edition asparagus green is number 58, defined as pistachio green mixed with much greyish white [6]. His three examples are the wings of the brimstone butterfly, the leaves of the variegated horse-shoe geranium *Pelargonium zonale*, and the mineral beryl [6]. Beryl is the species that also gives [[gem:emerald|emerald]] its name [6]. The name appears in several other lists printed by Baty: Lenz, Cleaveland in 1816 with 80 colours, and Syme's editions of 1814 and 1821 [2].

sections.title: Four systems, one name
sections.body:
Our library carries four sources for the name. The Werner swatch is an aged plate, so its color is approximate [7]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 records the term as first used in 1805, on plate 19 C 3 [7]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it in block 121, and Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXII shows a near-duplicate, Light Turtle Green, at a distance of only 1.0 [7].

The swatch is a light, muted yellow-green, lightness 77 and chroma 26, closest to [[khaki]] at 6.6 [7]. A modern survey color called Asparagus is much stronger, chroma 50, and a freshly cut spear is nearer that [7]. So the historical asparagus green is the greyed, milky side of the vegetable, in line with Syme's "much greyish white" [6][7]. Its neighbors are [[pistachio]], [[olive-green]], [[siskin-green]] and [[apple-green]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
At least five per cent of the canvas within a color distance of six, the swatch appears in 728 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 3.1 per cent, as photographed [8]. It is more common than average in the 1800s, with a lift of 1.4 over the same museums' baseline [8].

Some painters return to it again and again. It appears in 17 of 50 paintings by Arnoud van Halen, 11 of 28 by [[painter:paulus-potter|Paulus Potter]] and 5 of 12 by [[painter:johan-hendrik-weissenbruch|Weissenbruch]] [8]. The colors that keep it company are [[khaki]], [[sage]] and [[moss]] [8]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test [8].

How did Syme's 1821 edition define asparagus green?

questions.answer: Pistachio green mixed with much greyish white

questions.q: Historical asparagus green is as strong a green as a fresh spear.

openers: Asparagus green was a mineralogist's name: Syme's 1821 plate shows it on a butterfly's wing, a geranium leaf and a beryl.
The historical color is a chalky, greyed green, much quieter than the vegetable.

issues: Removed unsupported claim that the term entered geologists' vocabularies.
Removed folk-name gloss on sparrow-grass (not from sources).
